The answer rests in the underlying question here; what sort of future are you envisioning when you ask this kind of question? When people ask questions like the one in this thread, they're very often implying a dystopian future. They're often really asking; "How can we waste kids' time making them chase MBAs when the skills that will really matter are the survival skills --to hunt and fish and make stylish gladiatorial outfits from recycled car parts for when they're fighting in the Thunderdome?" Perhaps a better question is; are we equipping our children for the likely future, merely benignly wasting their time, or setting them up for failure or disaster?

As an amateur futurist, my take is that we're most-likely benignly wasting kids' time. Right now, our culture is suffering from a severe disconnect from the likely future, in part because the pace and comprehensiveness of change is go great but also partly because, under the Cold War, we've spent the past couple of generations in perpetual anticipation of imminent apocalypse and turned our collective back on the future, losing ourselves in nostalgia, fantasy, hedonism, nihilism, religion, and New Age baloney. Anything to distract from the dystopia or apocalypse we commonly assume must be around the corner. The end of the world didn't happen. The Berlin Wall fell. Now we're stuck with the bill for the excesses of the 20th century and don't know what to think. We don't know how to visualize the future anymore. Heaven and Hell are both on-offer, so we're told. The real danger--the real crime--is not in what we teach kids but in the debts we are imposing on them in the process. Education has always been 'worth it' to society. There's no 'wrong' education. But, on an individual level, we've created a situation where it ends up being erroneously measured in a context of return on investment with, at present, a shrinking margin that has reached a crisis point. Higher education has been reduced to the accreditation of class status for a job market that is so hyper-proletarianized that all companies really care about is class as an indicator of likely employee behavior and work-culture compatibility to justify their investment in job training.

I think the big disconnect between education and the future is in the need for more self-reliance, a broader technical/industrial literacy, an entrepreneurial and autodidactic mentality, as we approach a disruptive era where the nature of economics, business, industry, and careers are in great flux with the impact of automation and AI. No particular skill matters. It's a mentality that matters. A mentality that can surf change. We are entering a fourth stage of industrialization where production is demassifying, localizing, going on-demand, because the tools of production are becoming generalized, networked, and shrinking in scale and cost. 'Tooling' for production is disappearing. The cost of money is now the chief drag on competitiveness. And so the premises upon which capitalism are based are under strain, putting the nature of capitalism in flux. It may collapse. It may become something new. But we can plainly see the directions the technology is pointing in its evolutionary trends. How does capitalism work when production enters the local community, the home, becomes a commodity of exponentially shrinking cost like the processing 'capacity' of a computer, becomes a municipal utility merging with the infrastructure of the built habitat? Your next car may be assembled at the dealership. Amazon may turn into a public utility --an internet of stuff. The next Apple may be a company that manufactures nothing with a handful of employees whose jobs primarily involve the cultivation of product 'spimes'. If UBI emerges, careers may become about 'social capital', replacing financial credit. This is the future I see that no one is being prepared for.
